open-question.question: The retry has to appear in the commit procedure's prose, which eleven skills follow as their own tool calls, and literally in the six fixed shell calls that inline the three steps plus the orchestrator's new commit call, each written out in full. open-question.recommendation: Every call stays literal and self-evident under the shell-literal rule, no function of the runner's own stands in front of a git command and no fifth tool runs git writes against the rule that git rides beside the call, the procedure's three steps keep their shape for the eleven followers, who copy the one shown loop as they copy its other commands, and the goal's per-write wording is met exactly; the extra lines land mostly in the sweep's per-section copy, and a sleep inside a compound call runs under this host's shell tool (checked here), so the host-refusal exposure is not real.
open-question.alternative: Each git write gets its own bounded shell loop written out literally: in every one of the seven fixed calls (the sweep's batched call, both annotating passes' batch calls, the inline `complete-task` skill, `submit-task`, `derive-tasks`, and the orchestrator's new commit call) the `git add` line and the `git commit` line are each wrapped in a counted loop that repeats the write, pauses, and after the last attempt exits non-zero with git's message left standing, so the surrounding `&&` chain and the call's `stopped at` / failed-commit reporting still see a failure. `commit-procedure.md` shows the same loop in steps 2 and 3, and the eleven skills following it write that loop into their own git tool calls. No function, helper, or new file is added; the guard (`git status`) stays outside any loop. Every call stays fully literal and self-evident, the shape the shell-literal invariant already protects: nothing is defined that a runner could rename or shorten, no new tool joins the stdlib-only set, and the fixed-call tests extract and run the calls exactly as written. The most text and the most copies: two loops per commit across seven calls (per section in the sweep's batched call, per file in the alternatives loop) and in the procedure, each needing an explicit fail-after-the-bound construct because a plain `until`/`for` loop exits zero, so the copies can drift and every call grows hard to read; and if the pause the retry schedule sibling settles is a shell `sleep`, a host whose shell tool refuses a foreground sleep may refuse the call.

The retry is written literally once per commit rather than once per write: in each of the seven fixed calls one bounded loop wraps the `git add … && git commit …` pair as a unit (the guard stays before it), repeating the pair on failure, pausing between attempts, and exiting non-zero with git's message after the last attempt. `commit-procedure.md` shows the same single loop spanning its steps 2 and 3, and the eleven skills following it write that loop around their own add-and-commit call. Nothing is defined and no tool is added. Half the loop text of a per-write loop while staying fully literal: one retry per commit to read and keep in sync, and a commit that fails after its `git add` landed simply re-stages, which is harmless because both writes are path-scoped and idempotent. It departs from the goal's per-write wording (the retry wraps a sequence, not each git write), forces the procedure's separate stage and commit steps to be run as one chained call by every prose follower, and still repeats a fail-after-the-bound loop in seven calls plus the procedure, with the same exposure to a host refusing a shell `sleep` if the retry schedule sibling settles on one.

Each of the seven fixed calls opens by defining one small shell function that runs its arguments, repeats them on failure a bounded number of times with a pause, and returns git's exit status and message after the last attempt; every `git add` and `git commit` line in the call is then written as that function followed by the literal git command, path list and pathspec unchanged. `commit-procedure.md` shows the same definition and the wrapped form, and the eleven skills following it define and use the function in their own git tool calls. No tool is added. The bound and the pause are written once per call rather than at every write, so the many-section calls (the sweep's batched call, the alternatives loop) gain one definition instead of a loop per section, while each git command stays visible verbatim behind the wrapper. It introduces a runner-defined function standing in front of the commands, the very shape the shell-literal invariant bans for the open-question tool, so that invariant's scoping has to be reworded to sanction it, and prose followers that each define the function in their own calls are the runners most likely to paraphrase it; the definition is still copied into seven calls and the procedure, and a shell `sleep` pause, if the retry schedule sibling chooses one, carries the same host-refusal exposure.

The two sites take different forms. `commit-procedure.md` states the retry as runner behaviour, not shell text: when a `git add` or `git commit` tool call fails, the runner issues the same call again as a new tool call, up to the bound, before passing git's message on, so the eleven skills following the procedure carry no loop, function, or pause construct in their commands. The seven fixed calls, which run unattended in one shell process, carry a literal bounded loop around each git write as in the per-write loop option. The prose followers' commands stay exactly the plain guard, `git add`, and `git commit` they are today, with nothing for a runner to transcribe wrongly, and the turn between two tool calls is itself the pause, so no shell `sleep` reaches those commands. The retry then has two forms whose bounds and pauses are stated in different words and can diverge, the prose form spends a model turn per attempt and depends on the runner noticing the failure and counting its attempts, which is the kind of discretion the fixed calls exist to remove; how the runner tells a failure worth repeating depends on the retry trigger sibling's outcome.

A new stdlib-only, self-contained tool under `tools/` (Python 3.9+, importing no sibling, rendered byte-identical into every host) runs one git write given as its arguments, repeats it on failure a bounded number of times with the pause done inside the process, and on the last failure passes git's stderr and exit status through unchanged. open-question.question: A git write can fail for reasons other than a lock, such as a hook refusing the commit or a pathspec matching no file, and repeating a failed write lands nothing. Does a write repeat on every non-zero exit, with the runner reading nothing of git's message, or only when git's message names the lock it could not take?
open-question.recommendation: The retry reads nothing of git's output, so no captured stderr, English wording, locale, or undocumented exit-code convention enters any of the seven calls or the procedure the eleven followers write by hand, and the plugin-wide rule that a runner never classifies an error's wording holds; the cost, a non-lock refusal waiting out a window of a few seconds and a refusing hook repeating about ten times, is bounded and lands nothing twice, while every message-matching form puts a wording test where the procedure is followed by hand and exit 128 alone still covers a missing pathspec and a sandbox refusal.
open-question.alternative: Every git write (`git add`, `git commit`) repeats on any non-zero exit, whatever its code or message. Nothing of git's output is read or matched, by the runner or by the call. Once the bound is spent, the last attempt's message passes on unchanged. This is the position the draft `ideas/milestones_addressed_by_path.md` takes. It is the simplest trigger to write at all seven sites and in the commit procedure's prose. It needs no captured stderr and no pattern that git's wording or locale could break, and it fits the plugin-wide convention that a runner never classifies an error's wording. A failed write lands nothing, so a repeat never commits twice. Every failure that is not about a lock waits out the whole retry window before it surfaces: a hook refusing the commit, nothing to commit, a commit pathspec matching no file (all exit 1), and a missing `git add` pathspec (exit 128). A refusing pre-commit hook runs once per attempt, so any side effects it has, such as formatting or stashing files, repeat. How long the wasted wait lasts depends on the attempt count and pause the Retry schedule question sets.

A write repeats only when git exits with 128, its fatal-error code, which is the code a held `index.lock` produces. Exit 1 passes on at once: a hook refusal, nothing to commit, or a commit pathspec matching no file. The exit status is the only thing tested, and no message text is read. It skips the retry for the common non-lock refusals: hooks, empty commits, and `git commit`'s pathspec miss. It still reads nothing of git's message, so it needs no captured stderr and no wording-dependent pattern, and a test of `$?` is as easy to write in a fixed call as any non-zero test. 128 is not specific to the lock. `git add` with a pathspec matching no file exits 128 (checked here with git 2.50.1), and so do other fatal errors, such as a permission refusal on `.git`, which Codex's read-only sandbox can produce. All of these still wait out the window. The rule also depends on an exit-code convention that git does not document as a contract for each failure.

A write repeats only when git's captured message names the index lock as held, matching the `Unable to create '….git/index.lock': File exists.` form. Every other failure passes on at once on its first attempt, ref-lock failures on `git commit` included, which are left to git's own default ref-lock wait. Only the one contention git does not wait on at all, the index lock, is retried. Every other refusal, including a missing pathspec or a sandbox's `Operation not permitted` on the same lock path, surfaces immediately with git's message, and a refusing hook runs exactly once. Each write's stderr has to be captured and matched against git's English wording, which a translated locale or a future git release could change. Wherever a runner follows the commit procedure by its own tool calls, the match becomes a reading of the message, which cuts against the convention that a runner never classifies an error's wording. Two runs committing to one branch at once can still fail on the ref lock or a moved HEAD after git's default tenth of a second. How the match is written depends on the form the Retry form in calls question chooses.

A write repeats only when git's captured message names a lock it could not take, either the index lock or a ref lock: the `Unable to create '….lock': File exists.` form for any lock file, or the `cannot lock ref` form, which also covers a branch moved by another run's commit. Every other failure passes on at once on its first attempt. This covers every contention two runs in one tree can produce at a write, including the commit's update of the shared branch ref, which git waits on for only a tenth of a second. Hooks, empty commits, missing pathspecs, and permission refusals still surface immediately and run once. It carries the widest pattern to keep correct against git's English wording, a broader dependence on message text than the index-only match, with the same tension against the convention that a runner never classifies an error's wording wherever the procedure is followed by hand. A `cannot lock ref` that comes from a genuinely broken ref is retried for nothing. How the match is written depends on the form the Retry form in calls question chooses.

The text check asserts the retry's presence, not its behaviour, so a call that carries the retry around the wrong line, or one that is malformed in a way the pattern still matches, passes. It also ties a test to the calls' wording, which the milestone's draft avoided for the sweep's call ("asserts nothing about its text"). What the check matches on depends on the Retry form question: a helper call is one fixed token, while a loop written out in full is a multi-line shape.

No test holds or creates `.git/index.lock`. One untimed check reads every fixed call from the rendered tree and asserts that each git write line in it carries the retry in the form the milestone settles on. Whether the retry recovers or stops at its bound is exercised only when the parallel test's two calls happen to collide. It needs no timer and adds no suite time spent waiting on a retry window, so it can never be flaky. It still catches a git write the retry was left off. No test ever shows that the retry absorbs a lock or ends on a stale one. A retry with a wrong condition, a pause that never elapses, or no bound passes every run, and the bound against a crashed process's lock goes unverified.

No test is added for the retry. The lock retry is exercised only when the goal's parallel test happens to make its two calls collide on `.git/index.lock`, and it is otherwise untested, now and with no later test planned. It adds nothing to the suite and keeps the milestone to the one parallel test its goal names, with no timing-sensitive case to maintain. Whether the retry recovers, stops at its bound, or is present at all in a given call is checked only by chance. A broken retry can pass every run and surface only in the field as a `FAILED` return or a call that hangs on a crashed process's lock. If the parallel test does collide and the retry is broken, that test fails intermittently, which makes the parallel test itself flaky.

open-question.question: The `environment`, `repo`, `git`, and `run_call` helpers that build an isolated git repository live inside `tests/test_sweep_batched_call.py`, `tests/conftest.py` carries no git fixture, and the suite's convention is one flat file per concern. Does the new parallel test share those helpers by moving them into `tests/conftest.py`, or carry its own copies?

recommendation.option: Own copies in the new test

open-question.recommendation: The suite's convention is one self-contained flat file per concern, which the compact-view test already followed by copying the batched-call test's helpers rather than sharing them, and the goal names one new test, so no passing test is edited and conftest keeps its stated scope of the four tools' fixtures; the isolation environment is a short fixed dictionary whose drift shows as a failing run, and a later milestone can extract a shared home once the git-building tests have settled, as the tools' own duplicated helpers are deferred.

alternative.id: Own copies in the new test

open-question.alternative: No sharing: the new parallel test file carries its own `environment` fixture (plugin-root variable, `python3` wrapper, isolated git config and fixed identity), its own `git` and `run_call` helpers, its own `repo` fixture seeding its two milestones, and its own fence-extraction helper; `tests/test_sweep_batched_call.py`, `tests/test_sweep_compact_view.py`, and `tests/conftest.py` stay exactly as they are. Follows the precedent the suite already set, where `test_sweep_compact_view.py` carries its own copies of `fenced_blocks`, `environment`, and `run_call` beside the batched-call test's, so each concern stays one self-contained flat file that reads alone, and no passing test is edited for a milestone whose goal names only one new test. The git-isolation environment (`GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM`, the `/dev/null` global config, `HOME`, the fixed identity) exists in two copies that can drift apart, and a parallel test whose isolation silently differs from the sweep test's is exactly where a missed variable shows only on some machines; every further git-building test adds another copy, which depends on whether the lock-retry test coverage question adds a deterministic lock test of its own.

alternative.id: Conftest fixtures for the git tests

open-question.alternative: The four named helpers move into `tests/conftest.py`: `environment` as a fixture, `git` and `run_call` as module-level helpers or fixtures returning them, and `repo` generalized into a factory fixture taking which fixture milestones to seed (the pattern of the existing `milestone_dir` and `task_list_dir` factories), while the sweep-specific seeding stays in its own test; `test_sweep_batched_call.py` is rewritten to use them and the new parallel test uses them too, and `test_sweep_compact_view.py` keeps its own copies untouched. One home for the git-isolation environment under pytest's own sharing mechanism, the same one every tool fixture already uses, so both git-building tests run against the same isolation by construction and any later git test gets it for free. Edits a passing test outside the goal's stated scope and changes `conftest.py`'s declared purpose (its docstring scopes it to the four tools' suite), puts an `environment` fixture name in scope for every tool test that never touches git, and leaves the compact-view test's copies as a remaining duplicate, so the duplication is reduced rather than removed.

alternative.id: Conftest fixtures for every shell-call test

open-question.alternative: Every helper duplicated across the shell-call tests moves into `tests/conftest.py`: one `environment` fixture covering both existing variants (git isolation plus the dropped `BASH_ENV` and `ENV`), `git`, `run_call`, `fenced_blocks`, and a `repo` factory fixture; `test_sweep_batched_call.py` and `test_sweep_compact_view.py` are both rewritten to use them, and the new parallel test uses them as well. Removes the duplication outright, so every test that extracts a fixed call from the rendered tree and runs it under bash shares one extraction rule and one environment, and a fix to either lands once for all of them. The largest diff of the set, touching a test with no git in it and changing both existing tests' environments to the merged superset, which alters what two passing tests run under for a milestone that needs neither change, and the conftest grows a second, unrelated family of fixtures beside the tool fixtures it was written for.

alternative.id: Helper module for the git tests

open-question.alternative: The four named helpers move into a new plain module under `tests/` (for example `tests/shell_calls.py`, not collected because it is not named `test_*`), as functions the tests import explicitly, with `repo` generalized into a function taking the milestones to seed and each test file declaring its own thin fixtures over them; it is importable because the `tests/` directory carries no `__init__.py`, so pytest's default import mode puts it on `sys.path` (or by adding `tests` to the `pythonpath` line in `pyproject.toml`); `test_sweep_batched_call.py` and the new test import it, and `test_sweep_compact_view.py` and `conftest.py` stay untouched. Shares the git isolation between the two git-building tests while keeping `conftest.py` exactly the four tools' fixtures, and every use is an explicit import, so a reader of either test sees where each helper comes from rather than relying on implicit fixture injection. Introduces a new kind of file into a suite that is otherwise one flat `test_<name>.py` per concern plus `conftest.py`, rests on an import-path mechanism the suite has never relied on and that must hold under both the pinned and the 3.9 floor runs, and still edits a passing test while leaving the compact-view test's copies in place.

alternative.id: Helper module for every shell-call test

open-question.alternative: Every helper duplicated across the shell-call tests (`environment` in one merged form, `git`, `run_call`, `fenced_blocks`, and a `repo` builder taking the milestones to seed) moves into one new plain module under `tests/`, imported explicitly through the same import path as above; `test_sweep_batched_call.py` and `test_sweep_compact_view.py` are both rewritten to import from it, the new parallel test does too, and `conftest.py` stays untouched. Removes all the duplication across the rendered-call tests while keeping the tool fixtures' `conftest.py` unchanged and every shared helper an explicit, traceable import. Combines the costs of the widest refactor and the new file kind: both passing sweep tests are rewritten and run under a merged environment, the suite gains a non-test module and an import-path dependency it must keep working at the 3.9 floor, all for a milestone whose goal asks for one simple test.

open-question.question: The goal makes several complete-all-tasks runs able to share one working tree, but the scope gate that keeps two runs' cores apart belongs to a later milestone, and today's docs say the tree is clean after each skill (design claim 12) and that tasks run one at a time (claim 9). Do the docs present same-tree parallel runs as a supported way of using the plugin in this release, with a chain on the ways-of-using page and the claims reworded, or record only the commit mechanism and leave the capability unstated until the gate lands?
open-question.recommendation: The one same-tree concurrency the page already offers, preparing the next milestone beside a running completion, is exactly the leak this milestone closes and can be stated as safe now, and claim 12's clean-tree sentence is already false for that chain, so per-commit hygiene is the honest claim; two completion runs in one tree stay unstated because without the scope gate two agents can still edit one file at once and nothing but a sentence keeps their work apart, and the draft assigns claim 9 and the two-run chain to the gate's milestone, so stating them here would write an interim contract that milestone rewrites.
open-question.alternative: The docs cover only the same-tree concurrency they already describe. They record the pathspec, retry, and commit-from-file mechanism and state that the existing "Preparing the next milestone while the current one runs" chain no longer leaks a completion agent's files into the sweep's or a pass's commit. Claim 12 is reworded to per-commit hygiene, since a preparation run beside a live completion run already leaves the tree dirty. Claim 9 stays as written. Two `complete-all-tasks` runs in one tree are left unstated, and no new chain is added. It tells users the one parallel use the plugin already documents is now safe, and fixes claim 12 where it is already false today, without promising ungated parallel execution before the gate's milestone can back it. The milestone's headline purpose, several completion runs in one tree, ships with its mechanism and test but no user-facing statement. Claim 9 then sits beside a working capability it denies until the gate's milestone rewrites it.

The docs present same-tree parallel completion runs as supported in this release. `docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md` gains a chain that starts two `complete-all-tasks --milestone <milestone_id>` lines together in one working tree. Design claim 9 is reworded to one task at a time within a milestone, with several milestones' runs allowed side by side. Claim 12's "the work tree is clean after each skill" is reworded to per-commit hygiene: each commit records only its own paths, and the tree is clean once no other run is live. The chain's prose states the interim condition that, until the scope gate lands, the operator picks milestones whose work touches disjoint files. `docs/workflow.md` and the invariants record the pathspec, the retry, and the commit-from-file mechanism. The capability the milestone exists to deliver becomes visible and usable as soon as it ships, and the goal's own parallel test backs the claim. The docs also stop saying things that are false once two runs share a tree. The docs offer a recipe for parallel execution while the safeguard that keeps two runs' cores apart does not exist yet, so the only thing keeping the runs apart is a sentence the operator may skip. The draft's third milestone then rewrites claim 9 and the chain again around the gate, which means two edits of one contract.

The docs state same-tree parallel completion runs as supported, with no copy-paste chain. Claims 9 and 12 are reworded as in a full-support release: one task at a time within a milestone, and per-commit hygiene in place of a clean tree after each skill. One prose passage, in `docs/workflow.md` or the claims, says several milestones' `complete-all-tasks` runs may share one tree and that, until the scope gate lands, the operator keeps their work on disjoint files. `docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md` gains no chain. The mechanism is recorded as in every option. The claims say what is true of the release, and the capability is documented for anyone who reads for it, without the ways-of-using page's ready-to-run recipe inviting headless users into an ungated parallel run. It is a half-measure. A capability declared supported but given no chain on the page that collects the plugin's supported headless uses reads as hesitant, and the claim-9 rewording still has to be redone when the gate lands.

The docs record only the commit mechanism: the pathspec commit, the bounded retry, the agent's path file, and the orchestrator's commit-from-file. These go into `docs/workflow.md` `## How skills commit`, the `docs/skill-reference.md` entries, and the committing and return-contract invariants. Claim 12 changes only its staging wording, so the agent no longer stages, and keeps its clean-tree sentence. Claim 9 is untouched. No chain is added, and parallel runs are not mentioned. The capability is first stated when the gate lands. It is the smallest docs change. Every claim the docs make, and every chain they offer, keeps resting on a safeguard that exists, and the capability is described once, together with the gate that bounds it, with no interim wording to retire. The docs say nothing about a capability the release really has and its test exercises, and claim 12's clean-tree sentence stays false for the preparation chain the ways-of-using page already offers. A user who finds parallel runs on their own has no stated condition for doing it safely.

The docs record the commit mechanism, as in a mechanism-only release, and add an explicit statement, in claim 9 or beside the ways-of-using page's execution chain, that running two `complete-all-tasks` runs in one working tree is not supported until the scope gate lands. Claim 9 otherwise stands, claim 12 changes only its staging wording, and no chain is added. Nobody mistakes the new commit mechanism for permission to run ungated parallel execution. The docs keep the one-at-a-time promise and say plainly where its boundary lies until the gate exists. It disclaims the exact capability the milestone builds and tests, which leaves a negative statement in the docs that the gate's milestone must delete. It also discourages a use that is safe for milestones whose work is disjoint.
